items.title: Bill Huntington Interview, 1961-12-27
items.q: Through Bunk Johnson. ... I listened to Bunk and George and basically those people. Basically the album that Bunk put out... I used to listen to that album over and over again.

ctx.x: Well, what kind of music were you interested in when you were young?

Well, I heard nothing but classics until I was eight. And when I was eight, my sister introduced me to jazz. My sister was an opera singer, by the way. And she introduced me to jazz when I was about eight. Through Bunk Johnson. And my mother used to turn on the Metropolitan Opera ! But when she left the room, I'd switch over to a station that played Dixie in the afternoon. You know, the afternoon Metropolitan broadcast from New York. So that's how I became interested in jazz, basically. I was about eight then.…
Did your father play around the house?

items.title: Bill Huntington Interview, 1961-12-27
items.q: that guys like Bunke played with, you know, that, that same time feeling was this, actually it was the same time feeling that the modernists were playing with.

ctx.x: Sure. Yeah, just talk. Just say anything that comes to your mind. No, I'd rather not do that. . .

Well, uh, when I was about fifteen, uh, uh, actually through the efforts of Alvin Purnell. You see, I used to sit in with George Lewis and Alvin Purnell had a thing going where he'd play passing chords. And, uh, I was told when I was a kid that I had some kind of fantastic gear. I was some kind of child prodigy or something, you see. And so, uh, I'd hear all the things he was playing. And I'd tell Lawrence, why aren't you playing the same chords Alton's playing? You know, they sound like they're fitting more into…
Who did you like when you started playing? You mentioned Bonk, and then there must have been some other musicians. You said you met a lot on the mind.
